questions.question: A faulty weighing machine reads 1 kg when 900 gm is actually weighted on it. The shopkeeper marked the price of his goods by 10%, but unfortunately he was caught by the metrology department and then they ordered him to repair his weighing machine and gave punishment to sell the goods at 10% discount on cost price for a month. If each customer is now paying ₹20 for 1 kg, then before the raid _____ amount they have paid for the same quantity. (Rounded off to two places of decimal)
questions.questionHtml: A faulty weighing machine reads 1 kg when 900 gm is actually weighted on it. The shopkeeper marked the price of his goods by 10%, but unfortunately he was caught by the metrology department and then they ordered him to repair his weighing machine and gave punishment to sell the goods at 10% discount on cost price for a month. If each customer is now paying ₹20 for 1 kg, then before the raid _____ amount they have paid for the same quantity. (Rounded off to two places of decimal)
questions.solution:
Profit % = Profit/C.P. × 100 = 100/900 × 100 = 11.11%

Overall profit = 11.11 + 10 + (11.11 × 10)/100 = 22.22%

Actual Cost price of 1kg sugar = 100 /(100 - 10) × 20 = Rs22.22

So, Selling price = (100 + 22.22)/100 × 22.22 ≈ Rs27.16

questions.question: R’s weighing machine shows 400 gm when the actual weight is 350 gm. The cost price of almonds is ₹880 per kg and packets of 200 gm are made using the faulty machine. What should be the selling price (in ₹) of each packet to get a profit of 25%?
questions.questionHtml: R’s weighing machine shows 400 gm when the actual weight is 350 gm. The cost price of almonds is ₹880 per kg and packets of 200 gm are made using the faulty machine. What should be the selling price (in ₹) of each packet to get a profit of 25%?
questions.solution:
For every 400 gm, the actual weight is 350 gm

So for the 200 gm packet the actual weight = 200 × 350/400 = 175 gm

The CP of 175 gm = 880 × 175/1000 = 154

The selling price (in ₹) of each packet to get a profit of 25% = 154 × 125/100 = 154 × 5/4 = 192.50

questions.question: A shopkeeper claims to sell 450 kg rice at a cost price of ₹40 per kg but uses a weight of 900 grams instead of a one kilogram weight. He makes a profit of ₹2,520 by selling the remaining rice in the black market. The ratio of the black-market price to the original price per kg of rice is:
questions.questionHtml: A shopkeeper claims to sell 450 kg rice at a cost price of ₹40 per kg but uses a weight of 900 grams instead of a one kilogram weight. He makes a profit of ₹2,520 by selling the remaining rice in the black market. The ratio of the black-market price to the original price per kg of rice is:
questions.solution:
Given:

Cost price per kg = ₹40

Weight used = 900 grams (instead of 1 kg)

Total rice claimed to be sold = 450 kg

Profit made in the black market = ₹2,520

Formula used:

Weight actually sold = (Weight used/1000) × Total rice claimed to be sold

Remaining rice = Total rice - Weight actually sold

Black market price per kg = (Profit / Remaining rice)

Calculation:

Weight actually sold = (900/1000) × 450 = 0.9 × 450 = 405 kg

Remaining rice = 450 - 405 = 45 kg

Black market price per kg = Profit / Remaining rice = 2520 / 45

⇒ Black market price per kg = ₹56

Now, the ratio of the black-market price to the original price:

⇒ Ratio = 56 / 40 = 7 / 5

∴ The correct ratio of the black-market price to the original price is 7:5.

questions.question: During the lockdown, a state government gives 4.5 kg of rice to each person of a family at a cost price of ₹40 per kg. But the distributor uses false weight of 3.75 kg instead of 4.5 kg and distributes the rice. The accumulated rice was sold in the black market at double the price. He showed the government that he distributed 2700 kg of rice. When caught, he was made to pay a fine of 125% of what he earned in the black market. What was his fine amount?
questions.questionHtml: During the lockdown, a state government gives 4.5 kg of rice to each person of a family at a cost price of ₹40 per kg. But the distributor uses false weight of 3.75 kg instead of 4.5 kg and distributes the rice. The accumulated rice was sold in the black market at double the price. He showed the government that he distributed 2700 kg of rice. When caught, he was made to pay a fine of 125% of what he earned in the black market. What was his fine amount?
questions.solution:
Given:

Cost price of rice per kg = ₹40

Actual weight supposed to be given per person = 4.5 kg

Weight actually given per person = 3.75 kg

Price in black market = 2 × ₹40 = ₹80 per kg

Reported distribution = 2700 kg

Fine percentage = 125%

Formula Used:

1. Total rice actually distributed = (Reported distribution / Actual weight supposed to be given) × Weight actually given

2. Rice sold in black market = Reported distribution - Total rice actually distributed

3. Earnings from black market = Rice sold in black market × Price in black market

4. Fine amount = 125% of Earnings from black market

Calculation:

Reported distribution = 2700 kg

Actual weight supposed to be given = 4.5 kg

Weight actually given = 3.75 kg

⇒ Total rice actually distributed = (2700 / 4.5) × 3.75

⇒ Total rice actually distributed = 600 × 3.75

⇒ Total rice actually distributed = 2250 kg

Reported distribution = 2700 kg

Total rice actually distributed = 2250 kg

⇒ Rice sold in black market = 2700 - 2250

⇒ Rice sold in black market = 450 kg

Rice sold in black market = 450 kg

Price in black market = ₹80 per kg

⇒ Earnings from black market = 450 × 80

⇒ Earnings from black market = ₹36,000

Earnings from black market = ₹36,000

Fine percentage = 125%

⇒ Fine amount = (125 / 100) × 36,000

⇒ Fine amount = 1.25 × 36,000

⇒ Fine amount = ₹45,000

The correct answer is option 1.

questions.question: A shopkeeper normally makes a profit of 20% in a certain transaction; he weighed 900 gm instead of 1 kg due to an error in the weighing machine. If he charges 15% less than what he normally charges, then what is his actual profit or loss percentage?
questions.questionHtml: A shopkeeper normally makes a profit of 20% in a certain transaction; he weighed 900 gm instead of 1 kg due to an error in the weighing machine. If he charges 15% less than what he normally charges, then what is his actual profit or loss percentage?
questions.solution:
Given:

A shopkeeper normally makes a profit of 20% in a certain transaction; he weighed 900 gm instead of 1 kg due to an error in the weighing machine. If he charges 15% less than what he normally charges, then what is his actual profit or loss percentage?

Formula used:

Profit Percentage = \(\left(\dfrac{\text{Selling Price} - \text{Cost Price}}{\text{Cost Price}}\right) \times 100\)

Calculation:

Let the Cost Price (CP) of 1 kg be ₹100.

Selling Price (SP) with 20% profit = ₹120.

Due to the error, the shopkeeper weighs 900 gm instead of 1 kg. Hence, he sells 900 gm at 15% less than the normal price.

New Selling Price (NSP) = ₹120 × 0.85 = ₹102.

Effective Cost Price (ECP) of 900 gm = ₹90 (since 900 gm of ₹100/kg).

⇒ Profit = NSP - ECP = ₹102 - ₹90 = ₹12.

⇒ Profit Percentage = \(\left(\dfrac{12}{90}\right) \times 100\)

⇒ Profit Percentage = \(\dfrac{12}{90} \times 100 = 13.33\%\)

∴ The correct answer is option (1).

questions.questionHtml: A vendor sells his goods using weights 19% less than true weights and makes a profit of 35%. His net gain percentage (rounded off to 2 decimal places) is:
questions.solution:
Given:

The vendor uses weights that are 19% less than true weights and makes a profit of 35% on the selling price.

Step 1: Find the effective weight he is using.

Weight used = 100% - 19% = 81% of the true weight.

Step 2: To find the effective profit due to reduced weight:

Effective increase in price due to reduced weight = (100 / 81) - 1 = (100 - 81) / 81 = 19 / 81 = 0.2346 or 23.46%.

Step 3: Now, calculate the total profit.

Total profit = Profit due to reduced weight + Actual profit

Total profit = 23.46% + 35% + (23.46% × 35%) / 100

Total profit = 23.46 + 35 + (23.46 × 35) / 100

Total profit = 23.46 + 35 + 8.211

Total profit = 66.671%

∴ The net gain percentage is 66.67% (rounded off to 2 decimal places).

⇒ Let the false weight used by the shopkeeper for 1 kg be x grams.

⇒ When false weight is used,

⇒ Selling Price = Cost Price = Rs 100 and Profit = 25%

⇒ Cost price for 1000 grams rice = Rs 100

⇒ So, the Cost price for 1 gram of rice = \(\frac{100}{1000}=\frac{1}{10}\) Rs

⇒ For x grams, Cost Price of rice = \(\frac{x}{10}\) Rs

Putting the values in the formula,

⇒ \(\frac{SP-CP}{CP}\times 100=25\)

⇒ SP – CP = 0.25CP

⇒ SP = 1.25CP = \(1.25\times \frac{x}{10}\)

⇒ x = \(\frac{100\times 10}{1.25}=800\) grams.

⇒ Therefore, the amount of rice given in 1 kg = 800 grams

∴ The amount of rice given in 1 kg measurement is 800 grams.

questions.question: A dishonest dealer sells articles at 15% loss on cost price but uses the weight of 20 g instead of 25 g. What is his profit or loss percentage?
questions.questionHtml: A dishonest dealer sells articles at 15% loss on cost price but uses the weight of 20 g instead of 25 g. What is his profit or loss percentage?
questions.solution:
Given:

A dishonest dealer sells articles at 15% loss on cost price.

Concept:

Loss = Cost price - Selling price

Formula used:

\(P\%={SP-CP\over CP}× 100\)     Where, P = Profit, SP = Selling price, and CP = Cost price

Calculation:

Let the cost price of the 25 g article be X.

The selling price of the article = \({(1\ -\ {15\over 100})}\ × X={({100-15\over100})}\ × X={85\over100}\ × X=0.85X\)

The cost price of the 20g article = \({X\over 25}\ × 20={4X\over5}\)

The profit percentage = \({0.85X-0.8X\over0.8X}× 100={0.05X\over 0.8X}× 100={0.0625\ × 100}=6.25\%\)

∴ The required result will be 6.25% Profit.

questions.question: A dishonest dealer claims to sell his products at 24% loss on the cost price but uses 100 g weight instead of 200 g weight. His profit percentage is:
questions.questionHtml: A dishonest dealer claims to sell his products at 24% loss on the cost price but uses 100 g weight instead of 200 g weight. His profit percentage is:
questions.solution:
Shortcut Trick

Net Multiplier = (Weight Ratio) × (Price Factor)

Weight Ratio = True weight / False weight = 200 / 100 = 2

Price Factor = (100 − 24) / 100 = 0.76

Net Multiplier = 2 × 0.76 = 1.52

Profit = 1.52 − 1 = 0.52

∴ The correct option is B.

Alternate Method

Given:

⇒ Nominal weight = 200 g

⇒ Claimed loss = 24%

⇒ Actual weight used = 100 g

Formula Used:

Selling Price (SP) = CP × (100 ± Gain or Loss%)/100

Profit% = (SP − Effective CP) / Effective CP × 100

Calculations:

⇒ Let Cost Price (CP) of 1 g = 1 unit.

⇒ CP of 200 g = 200 units.

⇒ Dealer claims 24% loss, so SP = 200 × (100 − 24)/100 = 152 units.

⇒ Dealer delivers only 100 g, so Effective CP = 100 units.

⇒ Total Profit = SP − Effective CP = 152 − 100 = 52 units.

⇒ Profit percentage = (52 / 100) × 100 = 52%.

⇒ Profit in decimal form = 0.52.

∴ The correct option is B.

Additional Information

Dishonest Dealer Weight Formula

When a dealer sells at cost price but uses a false weight, Profit% = [ (Error) / (True Weight − Error) ] × 100.

Combined Profit with Weight and Price Change

Total Multiplier = (True Weight / False Weight) × (100 ± Profit or Loss%)/100. If result > 1, it is profit; if < 1, it is loss.

Marked Price and Dishonesty

If a dealer marks up by x% and uses a false weight, net gain = [ (100 + x) × (True weight / False weight) ] − 100.

questions.question: A shopkeeper sells his goods using weights 27% less than true weights and claims to sell his goods at the cost price. His gain per cent (rounded off to 1 decimal place) is:
questions.questionHtml: A shopkeeper sells his goods using weights 27% less than true weights and claims to sell his goods at the cost price. His gain per cent (rounded off to 1 decimal place) is:
questions.solution:
Given:

A shopkeeper sells his goods using weights 27% less than true weights and claims to sell his goods at the cost price.

Formula Used:

Gain % = (Gain / Cost Price) × 100

Calculation:

Let the true weight be 100 units.

Since the shopkeeper uses weights 27% less than the true weight:

Used weight = 100 - 27 = 73 units

He sells 73 units as 100 units.

Let the cost price of 1 unit be ₹1.

So, the cost price of 73 units = ₹73

Selling price of 73 units (since he claims to sell at cost price) = ₹100

Gain = Selling Price - Cost Price

Gain = ₹100 - ₹73 = ₹27

Gain % = (Gain / Cost Price) × 100

Gain % = (27 / 73) × 100

⇒ Gain % = (27)/(73) × 100

⇒ Gain % ≈ 36.9863

⇒ Gain % ≈ 37.0 (rounded off to 1 decimal place)

The gain per cent is 37.0%.

questions.question: A dishonest dealer sells an article at a 10% loss on the cost price but uses a weight of 40 g instead of 50 g. What is his percentage of profit?
questions.questionHtml: A dishonest dealer sells an article at a 10% loss on the cost price but uses a weight of 40 g instead of 50 g. What is his percentage of profit?
questions.solution:
Given:

A dishonest dealer sells an article at a 10% loss on the cost price but uses a weight of 40 g instead of 50 g.

Formula used:

Profit Percentage = \(\left(\dfrac{S.P. - C.P.}{C.P.}\right) \times 100\)

Calculation:

Let the cost price of 50 g be ₹100.

Selling price of 50 g at a 10% loss = ₹100 - 10% of ₹100

⇒ S.P. = ₹100 - ₹10

⇒ S.P. = ₹90

But dealer uses 40 g instead of 50 g, so he sells 40 g at ₹90.

Cost price of 40 g = \(\dfrac{100}{50} \times 40 = ₹80\)

Profit = S.P. - C.P.

⇒ Profit = ₹90 - ₹80

⇒ Profit = ₹10

Profit Percentage = \(\left(\dfrac{10}{80}\right) \times 100\)

⇒ Profit Percentage = 12.5%

∴ The correct answer is option (1).
